title: A frozen 1951-2004 degree-day model kept 0.26-0.28 skill for 2005-2024 US county corn and soybean yields; a generic climate screen called them unforecastable because of the yield trend
abstract: Question: does a pre-registered training-only forecastability screen (the shifted-climate false-signal rate, FSR, of sci:sha256:8804b69f) classify US county crop yields correctly, and does a published process-form relation keep forecast skill? Approach: we timestamped a plan before any yield statistic. Part A ran the dropped crop family of 8804b69f (4,263 county series of corn, soybeans and winter wheat, USDA NASS; train to 2004, test 2005-2024) through its unchanged engine. Part B froze a Schlenker-Roberts degree-day model (county effects, state trends, degree days above 29/30 C, precipitation; nClimGrid-daily) on 1951-2004 for 1,566 corn and 1,387 soybean counties, and forecast 2005-2024 with frozen weather slopes and a trend level refitted on the 15 previous years. Results: crop FSR was 0.49; the 13-unit line of 8804b69f predicted the forward skill of signalled series (-0.157 predicted, -0.152 observed), and the gate correctly chose the trailing mean for that engine. But the degree-day model beat the updated trend by 0.280 (95% block interval 0.097-0.428) for corn and 0.258 (0.208-0.332) for soybeans, 88-89% of the training weather signal, and beat the engine by 0.43-0.66. Across 51 state-crop units, forward skill rose with the training signal (Spearman 0.43, p = 0.0004). The corn heat coefficient fell from -0.68 to -0.47 per 100 degree days above 29 C; soybeans did not change. Frozen terms missed the 0.17 log-unit corn level rise. Exploratory: removing the training trend lowered crop FSR to 0.22, and the gate then chose the climate model correctly. Limitations: observed weather, county-average temperatures, pooled irrigated and rain-fed fields, one extreme year (2012), and a weather-join bug that we found and fixed after a debug run.
